```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.align = "center")
source("../R/utils.R")
for (f in list.files(repo_path("R"), pattern = "[.]R$", full.names = TRUE)) source(f)
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(caret)
  library(survey)
})
started <- Sys.time()
threads <- n_threads()
seed <- 5330
```

This notebook fits five classifiers for self-reported diagnosed diabetes using
2024 BRFSS predictors, then evaluates them once on a held-out test set. All
preprocessing that estimates anything from data (median imputation, scaling,
the k-means risk-profile cluster) is fit on the training rows only.

## 1. Data and cohort

```{r load}
raw <- data.table::fread(repo_path("data", "brfss2024_extract_slim.csv.gz"), data.table = FALSE)
state_names <- c(`1` = "Alabama", `2` = "Alaska", `4` = "Arizona", `5` = "Arkansas",
                 `6` = "California", `8` = "Colorado", `9` = "Connecticut", `10` = "Delaware",
                 `11` = "District of Columbia", `12` = "Florida", `13` = "Georgia",
                 `15` = "Hawaii", `16` = "Idaho", `17` = "Illinois", `18` = "Indiana",
                 `19` = "Iowa", `20` = "Kansas", `21` = "Kentucky", `22` = "Louisiana",
                 `23` = "Maine", `24` = "Maryland")
stopifnot(all(as.character(unique(raw[["_STATE"]])) %in% names(state_names)))

analytic <- prepare_brfss(raw)
rf_trees <- 200
if (quick_run()) {
  set.seed(seed)
  analytic <- analytic[sample(nrow(analytic), 8000), ]
  rf_trees <- 50
}
excluded <- table(factor(raw$DIABETE4, levels = c(2, 7, 9)), useNA = "ifany")
n_raw <- nrow(raw)
n_analytic <- nrow(analytic)
prevalence <- mean(analytic$diabetes == "Yes")

weight_by_state <- aggregate(`_LLCPWT` ~ `_STATE`, data = raw, FUN = sum)
md_weight <- weight_by_state$`_LLCPWT`[weight_by_state$`_STATE` == 24] / 1e6
```

The file is the course-provided extract of the 2024 BRFSS combined landline and
cell phone data. It is **not the national file**: it holds
`r fmt_int(n_raw)` records from `r length(unique(raw[["_STATE"]]))` jurisdictions
(state FIPS 1 to 24, `r paste(state_names, collapse = ", ")`). Results describe
respondents in these jurisdictions only.

The extract appears to be the first part of the national file, cut off partway
through Maryland: Maryland's final weights sum to only `r fmt_num(md_weight, 2)`
million, far below its adult population, while the other jurisdictions look
complete. Maryland respondents are kept for modeling but excluded from the
survey-weighted estimates below.

The outcome is DIABETE4 = 1 ("ever told you have diabetes") versus 3 (no) or 4
(no, prediabetes or borderline). I excluded gestational-only diabetes
(code 2, n = `r fmt_int(excluded[["2"]])`), don't know (7, n = `r fmt_int(excluded[["7"]])`),
refused (9, n = `r fmt_int(excluded[["9"]])`) and blanks. The analytic cohort has
`r fmt_int(n_analytic)` respondents and an unweighted prevalence of
`r fmt_pct(prevalence)`.

Coding checks against the 2024 codebook, applied in `R/recode_brfss.R`:

- PHYSHLTH and MENTHLTH: 88 means zero days; 77 and 99 are set to missing.
- `_BMI5` has two implied decimals, so BMI = `_BMI5` / 100; blanks are missing.
- CHECKUP1 = 8 means "never had a routine checkup". The course version treated it
  as missing; here it is its own level.
- Calculated variables use 9 for don't know or missing; those, and 7/9 on the
  yes/no items, become an explicit `Missing` level.
- `_TOTINDA`, `_RFHLTH` and `_MICHD` are dropped because they are recodes of
  EXERANY2, GENHLTH and CVDINFR4/CVDCRHD4, which are already in the model. The
  agreement check below confirms the overlap.

```{r redundancy}
redundancy <- data.frame(
  derived = c("_TOTINDA", "_RFHLTH", "_MICHD"),
  source = c("EXERANY2", "GENHLTH", "CVDINFR4 or CVDCRHD4"),
  agreement = c(
    mean((raw$EXERANY2 %in% 1) == (raw$`_TOTINDA` %in% 1)),
    mean((raw$GENHLTH %in% 1:3) == (raw$`_RFHLTH` %in% 1)),
    mean((raw$CVDINFR4 %in% 1 | raw$CVDCRHD4 %in% 1) == (raw$`_MICHD` %in% 1))
  )
)
redundancy$agreement <- fmt_pct(redundancy$agreement, 3)
knitr::kable(redundancy, col.names = c("Dropped variable", "Derived from", "Rows that agree"))
```

## 2. Survey-weighted prevalence (context only)

The models below are unweighted predictive models: they learn from the sample as
drawn and are evaluated on held-out respondents. To put the sample prevalence in
context, I estimated weighted prevalence with the BRFSS design (strata `_STSTR`,
final weight `_LLCPWT`, one respondent per PSU) over the 20 complete jurisdictions.

```{r survey}
options(survey.lonely.psu = "adjust")
svy_data <- data.frame(state = raw[["_STATE"]], strata = raw[["_STSTR"]], psu = raw[["_PSU"]],
                       weight = raw[["_LLCPWT"]], diabete4 = raw$DIABETE4,
                       age65 = as.numeric(raw[["_AGE80"]] >= 65))
svy_data <- svy_data[svy_data$diabete4 %in% 1:4, ]
svy_data$cdc_definition <- as.numeric(svy_data$diabete4 == 1)
svy_data$model_definition <- ifelse(svy_data$diabete4 == 2, NA, svy_data$cdc_definition)
# In BRFSS each respondent is their own PSU (_PSU repeats the record number
# within a state). With one respondent per PSU, ids = ~1 gives the same
# linearized variance as ids = ~psu and runs in seconds instead of minutes.
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(svy_data[c("state", "psu")]))
design <- svydesign(ids = ~1, strata = ~strata, weights = ~weight, data = svy_data)
design_complete <- subset(design, state != 24)

estimate <- function(formula, dsn) {
  est <- svymean(formula, dsn, na.rm = TRUE)
  ci <- confint(est)
  c(estimate = unname(coef(est)), low = ci[1], high = ci[2])
}
prev_cdc <- estimate(~cdc_definition, design_complete)
prev_model <- estimate(~model_definition, design_complete)
unweighted_complete <- mean(analytic$diabetes[analytic$state_fips != 24] == "Yes")
age65_weighted <- estimate(~age65, design_complete)[["estimate"]]
age65_unweighted <- mean(svy_data$age65[svy_data$state != 24])

prev_table <- data.frame(
  definition = c("Diagnosed diabetes, DIABETE4 = 1 vs 2/3/4",
                 "Model outcome, DIABETE4 = 1 vs 3/4"),
  weighted = c(prev_cdc["estimate"], prev_model["estimate"]),
  low = c(prev_cdc["low"], prev_model["low"]),
  high = c(prev_cdc["high"], prev_model["high"])
)
write_table(prev_table, "brfss_weighted_prevalence")
knitr::kable(transform(prev_table, weighted = fmt_pct(weighted), low = fmt_pct(low),
                       high = fmt_pct(high)),
             col.names = c("Definition", "Weighted prevalence", "95% CI low", "95% CI high"))

by_state <- svyby(~model_definition, ~state, design, svymean, na.rm = TRUE)
by_state <- data.frame(state = state_names[as.character(by_state$state)],
                       weighted_prevalence = by_state$model_definition,
                       se = by_state$se,
                       note = ifelse(by_state$state == 24, "incomplete sample", ""))
write_table(by_state, "brfss_weighted_prevalence_by_state")
```

Weighted prevalence of the model outcome is `r fmt_pct(prev_model["estimate"])`
(95% CI `r fmt_pct(prev_model["low"])` to `r fmt_pct(prev_model["high"])`), against
an unweighted `r fmt_pct(unweighted_complete)` in the same jurisdictions. Much of
the gap is age: `r fmt_pct(age65_unweighted)` of these respondents are 65 or older,
versus a weighted `r fmt_pct(age65_weighted)`. Predicted probabilities from the
unweighted models therefore reflect the sample, not the adult population.
State estimates are in `outputs/tables/brfss_weighted_prevalence_by_state.csv`.

## 3. Train/test split and train-only preprocessing

```{r split}
set.seed(seed)
train_idx <- createDataPartition(analytic$diabetes, p = 0.80, list = FALSE)[, 1]
train_raw <- analytic[train_idx, ]
test_raw <- analytic[-train_idx, ]

prep <- fit_preprocessor(train_raw, impute_vars = brfss_numeric_vars,
                         cluster_vars = brfss_numeric_vars,
                         cluster_name = "risk_profile_cluster", k = 3, nstart = 20, seed = seed)
train <- apply_preprocessor(prep, train_raw)
test <- apply_preprocessor(prep, test_raw)

base_predictors <- c(brfss_numeric_vars, names(brfss_factor_spec))
predictors <- c(base_predictors, "risk_profile_cluster")
y_train <- as.integer(train$diabetes == "Yes")
y_test <- as.integer(test$diabetes == "Yes")
missing_share <- vapply(train_raw[brfss_numeric_vars], function(x) mean(is.na(x)), numeric(1))
```

I split 80/20, stratified on the outcome (train n = `r fmt_int(nrow(train))`,
test n = `r fmt_int(nrow(test))`), before any imputation or clustering. Training
medians fill missing numeric values (BMI is missing for
`r fmt_pct(missing_share[["bmi"]])` of training rows). The k-means risk-profile
cluster (k = 3, 20 starts) is fit on standardized age, BMI and unhealthy days in
the training set; test respondents are assigned to the nearest training center.

```{r cluster-profile}
profile <- cluster_profile(prep, train)
profile$diabetes_rate_train <- fmt_pct(tapply(y_train, train$risk_profile_cluster, mean)[profile$cluster])
write_table(profile, "brfss_cluster_profile")
knitr::kable(profile, col.names = c("Cluster", "Age", "BMI", "Phys. days", "Ment. days",
                                    "Train n", "Diabetes rate"))
```

### PCA check

```{r pca}
pca_x <- model.matrix(reformulate(base_predictors), data = train)[, -1]
pca_x <- pca_x[, apply(pca_x, 2, sd) > 0]
pca <- prcomp(pca_x, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
pca_cum <- cumsum(pca$sdev^2) / sum(pca$sdev^2)
pca_90 <- which(pca_cum >= 0.90)[1]
```

On the dummy-coded training predictors, `r pca_90` of `r length(pca_cum)`
principal components are needed to explain 90% of the variance, so PCA would
compress little and cost interpretability. I kept the original variables.

## 4. Models and cross-validation

All models share the same five stratified folds of the training set and are
tuned on cross-validated AUC.

```{r fit}
folds <- cv_folds(train$diabetes, k = 5, seed = seed)
fit_start <- Sys.time()
models <- classification_models(train, "diabetes", predictors, folds, threads,
                               rf_trees = rf_trees)
models$forest_no_cluster <- fit_ranger_fixed(train, "diabetes", base_predictors,
                                             tune = models$forest$bestTune,
                                             threads = threads, trees = rf_trees)
fit_minutes <- as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), fit_start, units = "mins"))
tree_leaves <- sum(models$tree$finalModel$frame$var == "<leaf>")

labels <- c(logistic = "Logistic regression", penalized = "Penalized logistic",
            tree = "Classification tree", forest = "Random forest",
            forest_no_cluster = "Random forest, no cluster")
colors <- model_colors(unname(labels))

cv_table <- data.frame(
  model = labels[c("logistic", "penalized", "tree", "forest")],
  cv_auc = vapply(models[c("logistic", "penalized", "tree", "forest")], cv_summary,
                  numeric(1), metric = "ROC"),
  tuning = vapply(models[c("logistic", "penalized", "tree", "forest")], tune_label, character(1))
)
write_table(cv_table, "brfss_cv_results")
knitr::kable(transform(cv_table, cv_auc = fmt_num(cv_auc)), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Model", "5-fold CV AUC", "Selected tuning"))
```

The random forest uses `ranger` with `r rf_trees` trees; the no-cluster forest
reuses the tuned settings of the main forest and is trained on the same rows
without the cluster feature. The selected classification tree (cp =
`r models$tree$bestTune$cp`) has `r fmt_int(tree_leaves)` leaves.
`r if (tree_leaves > 30) "At this sample size a deep tree discriminates better than a shallow one, but it is no longer a short rule set someone could read, which was the reason for including a tree." else ""`
Model fitting took `r fmt_num(fit_minutes, 1)` minutes on `r threads` threads.

## 5. Held-out test performance

The decision threshold for each model is the highest cut-off that reaches 80%
sensitivity in that model's **out-of-fold training predictions**. I targeted
sensitivity because, for a screening use, a missed case (someone who never gets
an HbA1c test) costs more than an extra test. Choosing the threshold on training
data keeps the test set untouched until final scoring.

```{r test-metrics}
test_prob <- lapply(models, predict_prob, newdata = test)
oof <- lapply(models[c("logistic", "penalized", "tree", "forest")], oof_prob)

# The no-cluster forest was not cross-validated, so its threshold comes from its
# own out-of-bag training predictions, which are also out-of-sample.
oob_no_cluster <- models$forest_no_cluster$finalModel$predictions[, "Yes"]
thresholds <- c(vapply(oof, threshold_for_sensitivity, numeric(1), y01 = y_train, target = 0.80),
                forest_no_cluster = threshold_for_sensitivity(oob_no_cluster, y_train, 0.80))

test_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(models), function(m) {
  p <- test_prob[[m]]
  cbind(model = labels[[m]], auc_with_ci(p, y_test),
        average_precision = average_precision(p, y_test),
        brier = brier_score(p, y_test),
        confusion_metrics(p, y_test, thresholds[[m]]))
}))
test_table <- test_table[order(-test_table$auc), ]
write_table(test_table, "brfss_test_metrics")

show <- with(test_table, data.frame(
  Model = model,
  `AUC (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f to %.3f)", auc, auc_low, auc_high),
  `Avg. precision` = fmt_num(average_precision),
  Brier = fmt_num(brier, 4),
  Threshold = fmt_num(threshold),
  Sensitivity = fmt_num(sensitivity), Specificity = fmt_num(specificity),
  PPV = fmt_num(ppv), check.names = FALSE))
knitr::kable(show, row.names = FALSE)

brier_null <- brier_score(rep(mean(y_train), length(y_test)), y_test)

roc_list <- lapply(test_prob, roc_object, y01 = y_test)
best <- names(labels)[match(test_table$model[1], labels)]
cmp_best <- pROC::roc.test(roc_list[[best]], roc_list$logistic, method = "delong", paired = TRUE)
cmp_cluster <- pROC::roc.test(roc_list$forest, roc_list$forest_no_cluster, method = "delong",
                              paired = TRUE)
comparisons <- data.frame(
  comparison = c(paste(labels[[best]], "vs Logistic regression"),
                 "Random forest vs Random forest, no cluster"),
  auc_difference = c(diff(rev(as.numeric(cmp_best$estimate))),
                     diff(rev(as.numeric(cmp_cluster$estimate)))),
  p_value = c(cmp_best$p.value, cmp_cluster$p.value)
)
write_table(comparisons, "brfss_auc_comparisons", digits = 6)
```

For reference, predicting the training prevalence for everyone gives a Brier
score of `r fmt_num(brier_null, 4)` on this test set. The best Brier score,
`r fmt_num(min(test_table$brier), 4)`, is a `r fmt_pct(1 - min(test_table$brier) / brier_null)`
reduction from that baseline.

Paired DeLong tests on the test set:

```{r comparisons}
knitr::kable(transform(comparisons, auc_difference = fmt_num(auc_difference, 4),
                       p_value = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3, eps = 1e-4)),
             col.names = c("Comparison", "AUC difference", "p value"))
```

```{r roc-figure}
roc_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(roc_list), function(m) {
  r <- roc_list[[m]]
  data.frame(model = labels[[m]], sensitivity = rev(r$sensitivities),
             specificity = rev(r$specificities))
}))
auc_lookup <- setNames(sprintf("%s (AUC %.3f)", test_table$model, test_table$auc), test_table$model)
roc_df$model <- factor(auc_lookup[as.character(roc_df$model)], levels = auc_lookup[unname(labels)])
p_roc <- plot_roc(roc_df, setNames(colors, auc_lookup[names(colors)]),
                  title = "ROC curves, held-out test set",
                  subtitle = sprintf("BRFSS 2024, 21 jurisdictions, n = %s test respondents",
                                     fmt_int(length(y_test))))
save_figure(p_roc, "brfss_roc_curves", width = 7, height = 6.5)
knitr::include_graphics(figure_link("brfss_roc_curves"))
```

```{r pr-figure}
pr_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(test_prob), function(m) {
  cbind(model = labels[[m]], pr_curve(test_prob[[m]], y_test))
}))
pr_df <- pr_df[pr_df$recall > 0, ]  # precision is undefined before the first case
pr_df$model <- factor(pr_df$model, levels = unname(labels))
p_pr <- plot_pr(pr_df, colors, prevalence = mean(y_test),
                title = "Precision-recall curves, held-out test set")
save_figure(p_pr, "brfss_precision_recall", width = 7, height = 5.5)
knitr::include_graphics(figure_link("brfss_precision_recall"))
```

With about one positive in seven, precision is the harder number. At the
80%-sensitivity threshold the best model flags `r fmt_pct(test_table$flagged[1])`
of test respondents, and `r fmt_pct(test_table$ppv[1])` of those flagged have
diagnosed diabetes.

```{r calibration-figure}
cal_models <- c("logistic", "penalized", "tree", "forest")
cal_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cal_models, function(m) {
  cbind(model = labels[[m]], calibration_bins(test_prob[[m]], y_test, bins = 10))
}))
cal_df$model <- factor(cal_df$model, levels = unname(labels[cal_models]))
write_table(cal_df, "brfss_calibration_deciles")
p_cal <- plot_calibration(cal_df, colors[unname(labels[cal_models])],
                          title = "Calibration, held-out test set")
save_figure(p_cal, "brfss_calibration", width = 10, height = 3.6)
knitr::include_graphics(figure_link("brfss_calibration"))
```

## 6. Which predictors matter

Permutation importance is the drop in test AUC when one predictor is shuffled.
It is computed the same way for the logistic model and the random forest, so the
two can be compared on one scale.

```{r importance}
auc_metric <- function(y, p) as.numeric(pROC::auc(roc_object(p, y)))
imp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("logistic", "forest"), function(m) {
  pf <- function(d) predict_prob(models[[m]], d)
  cbind(model = labels[[m]],
        permutation_importance(pf, test, y_test, predictors, auc_metric, seed = seed))
}))
imp$model <- factor(imp$model, levels = unname(labels[c("logistic", "forest")]))
write_table(imp, "brfss_permutation_importance", digits = 5)
p_imp <- plot_importance(imp, colors[unname(labels[c("logistic", "forest")])],
                         title = "Predictor importance for diagnosed diabetes",
                         x_label = "Drop in test AUC when shuffled")
save_figure(p_imp, "brfss_permutation_importance", width = 9, height = 5)
knitr::include_graphics(figure_link("brfss_permutation_importance"))
top_logistic <- head(imp$variable[imp$model == labels[["logistic"]]], 4)
top_forest <- head(imp$variable[imp$model == labels[["forest"]]], 4)
```

## 7. Summary

- Best test AUC: `r test_table$model[1]`, `r fmt_num(test_table$auc[1])`
  (95% CI `r fmt_num(test_table$auc_low[1])` to `r fmt_num(test_table$auc_high[1])`).
  Logistic regression reached `r fmt_num(test_table$auc[test_table$model == labels[["logistic"]]])`.
- The k-means cluster changed random forest test AUC by
  `r fmt_num(comparisons$auc_difference[2], 4)` (DeLong p = `r format.pval(comparisons$p_value[2], digits = 3, eps = 1e-4)`).
- Top predictors by permutation importance: `r paste(top_logistic, collapse = ", ")`
  (logistic) and `r paste(top_forest, collapse = ", ")` (random forest).
- These are associations in cross-sectional survey data. A respondent who
  already knows they have diabetes may report worse health or more checkups
  because of the diagnosis, so the model describes who reports diabetes rather
  than who will develop it.

```{r runtime}
runtime <- as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), started, units = "mins"))
```

Notebook runtime: `r fmt_num(runtime, 1)` minutes.
